utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday. Good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel, all the OTP representatives, and good afternoon to all the people assisting us. First of all, I'll ask Mr. Registrar to give us an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 4D has submitted his objection to documents tendered through witness Marijan Davor by 2D. This objection shall be given Exhibit IC0-0911. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Scott, I think you have a new member of your team you want to introduce to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours. I hope everyone had a good weekend. Good afternoon, Counsel, and all those in and around the courtroom. Yes, Your Honour, I'm very happy to -- to present to the Chamber this afternoon a new colleague who has joined us some time ago, but it's the first time that he's joined us in court. His name is Simon Laws, and L-a-w-s. So a good name for a lawyer. Mr. Laws comes from the Bar of England and Wales, where he is, I think, in his 18th year of practice, having been called to the Bar. In that system, he has done both prosecution and defence work. I hasten to add, as I normally do, given comments that are made from time to time about the size of the Prosecution case or the Prosecution team -- well, case and team, Your Honour, that the team has not gotten any larger, but unfortunately with the length of this case, people come and people go. The Chamber may or may not know Mr. Poryvaev left some time ago, and one or two other members of our staff who may or may not have been in court recently have left over the past six months. The team has not gotten larger, but we have had some changes. Mr. Laws is a very experienced trial lawyer, and the Chamber will be seeing him taking witnesses in court in the near future, and I'm happy to have him join us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. Well, Mr. Simon Laws, welcome, on behalf of the Trial Chamber. We are very happy to see you get on board in the OTP team in charge of this case. Welcome, again, and I'm sure that we'll have the pleasure in the coming days or weeks to hear you. Ms. Nozica, your witness is ready, I believe. Let's have him brought in. Mr. Usher, please. Well, I avail myself of this opportunity to welcome all the associates of Ms. Alaburic. Welcome to them, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to welcome -- thank you for your welcome. I have noticed that you have looked at my associates with interest. They're not in the courtroom for the first time, but I can introduce them. They are legal assistants in the General Petkovic Defence team, Ms. Natalija Labavic, who is an intern in Zagreb, and Mrs. Sara Lustig who is studying at the University of Law in New York.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope you can hear me. Could you please state your surname, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Slobodan Bozic. I was born on the 2nd of November, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a lawyer by profession. At the moment, I'm working in a company as a lawyer, and I'm working in the human resources department of that company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you had an opportunity to testify before an international or domestic court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is this going to be the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have never testified before, before any court. I was questioned or interrogated by The Hague Tribunal in the capacity of a suspect, but I never actually learned why this happened. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me give you some explanation. You are a lawyer, so what I'm about to say is not going to be of any surprise to you. In these proceedings, you are going to be first put questions by Ms. Nozica, as the Defence counsel of Mr. Stojic; and she's about to ask questions of you, following which the other Defence lawyers seated on your left, defending the other accused, may also ask questions as part of their cross-examination. After that, the Office of the Prosecutor, who's represented by the people on your right-hand side, is going to cross-examine you and will be given the same amount of time as the time needed for examination-in-chief. The four Judges in front of you can also ask questions of you, depending, of course, on the documents or the questions put to you, but we'll be very mindful not to take up too much of the time because we realise, based on the latest statistics established by the Registrar, we took up too much time. Therefore, we're going to exercise self-restraint and make sure that we do not step in too often. Also endeavour to be very precise in your answers. If you fail to understand anything, do not hesitate to ask the person asking you the question to rephrase it. We shall break every hour and a half for 20 minutes for you to have a rest and also so that the audio and videotapes can be changed. You have just taken an oath. Therefore, as of now you're not to have any contact whatsoever with the Stojic Defence team or with other Defence counsel, or with the OTP, for that matter, because now you are a witness of the Court; so that when you go back to your hotel, you're not supposed to talk to anyone about the progress of the case unless of course you want to speak to your companion, to your wife, just to say that everything is going fine. Ms. Nozica must have told you this. She has a specific number of hours for her examination-in-chief. The same for the other Defence counsel. So you are going to spend at least two weeks here. I hope you made all the necessary arrangements. So this is what I wanted to tell you. Ms. Nozica, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I would like to make a note that we have provided a new schedule of witnesses, and according to that, we plan this witness to be finished by next Tuesday because we have already planned a new witness for Wednesday and Thursday. We know it's too early to make any firm decisions about this, and I do need to call the new witness, so probably at the end of the day on Thursday we will know what our schedule will be after that. Your Honours, since we're talking about a witness, Mr. Bozic, who's going to be examined in chief by the Defence of Mr. Stojic, too, and the Defence of Mr. Praljak, if necessary do we need to instruct the witness about the course of the examination-in-chief? You have instructed the witness about the examination of him by the Stojic Defence, but I think that he also needs to be instructed about his examination-in-chief by the Praljak Defence. I think perhaps we need to make that information available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it so happens that General Praljak plans to put questions to you. We, the Trial Chamber, agree to that, but General Praljak and his lawyer will intervene following Ms. Nozica's examination, once she has completed her examination-in-chief. So General Praljak will intervene after her. This is the way things have been scheduled. General Praljak can ask questions. If you mention parts in your testimony that relates to his expertise or his military knowledge, then he will ask the questions himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Your Honour, but I would like to ask a question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that I'm probably going to be in this courtroom for the next two weeks. Unfortunately, because of the fact that I couldn't start my testimony because the previous witness took longer, and in the meantime I'm having some problems with my eye; and thanks to a lot of help from the Victims and Witnesses Unit, I have managed to take care, to a degree, of my problem. However, I am here at the summons of the Court, and because of that I had to take two weeks' leave from work. If this should be extended, I will have to then enter into the third week. I'm working on assignments that have dead-lines at my job, so I would like to know what this means. Is there a kind of dead-line so that I could plan my duties according to my earlier plans, in view of the fact that my testimony is taking longer, but it was planned to take only six days? I would need to be back in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the following Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going to testify today, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, and on Thursday. You will return on Monday and Tuesday of next week. Why, sir? Because Ms. Nozica has scheduled a witness who is about to testify over two days. So if all goes well, you should be leaving The Hague next Tuesday, if all goes well. Of course, you never know. Sometimes things may come up which I can't foresee right now. So you're here for this week and for next Monday and Tuesday. That's the plan. You never know. It could be shorter, it could be longer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, if you have any questions, don't hesitate to address them to the Trial Chamber. It will be our pleasure to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon once again, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, you have given us your particulars in response to His Honour Judge Antonetti's question. I would like you to briefly tell us which schools you completed, where and when, and to very briefly tell us how you started working in your office job.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary and secondary education in Siroki Brijeg. I finished the Faculty of Law in Zagreb. After I served my military term of duty in the former state, I worked in the Municipal Court in Mostar as an intern, and then after passing my trial term of office, I passed the Bar exam in Sarajevo, and after that I was appointed a judge of the Municipal Court in Siroki Brijeg. After a while, I became the president of the Municipal Board of the League of Communists in Siroki Brijeg; and then after that I became the President of the Municipal Assembly or the mayor of Siroki Brijeg. And after my term of duty expired, I returned and became the local prosecutor for the Siroki Brijeg and Posusje municipalities. At the end of the 1980s, I became the chief of police of Herzegovina, which practically covered 17 municipalities in Herzegovina at the time, and currently some of these municipalities belong to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and some belong to the Republika Srpska. I was the chief of police in Mostar until the multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, when you say the post of chief of police in Mostar, can you explain to the Trial Chamber which municipalities that police organisation covered that you were at the head of and when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: It was the period from 1989 to mid-1991. These are municipalities, if you look from the south-east, from Trebinje, Bileca, Gackonje [phoen], Vesinje [phoen], Ljubinje, Neum, Capljina, Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor, Posusje, Grude, Ljubusko, Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, Siroki Brijeg. And what happened after that? Now we're talking about this period from 1989 to mid-1991. What happened in your professional life? After that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Sometime in June 1991, after -- a few months after the multiparty elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Lucic became the chief of police, and in agreement with the authorities that were in power at the time, I was supposed to remain as his adviser for another three months; but in the meantime, I actually opened my own law practice, which was under the jurisdiction of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Bar and began to work there after this work together ended after three months. Unfortunately, the three months in Bosnia -- in those three months, things happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina which prevented me from actually starting to work in my practice. I stayed in the police force because already in mid-1991 the Herzegovina, Mostar, Capljina and part of the Dubrava Plateau area was ran over by members of the JNA and the reservists of that same army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that post? And I'm going to ask you to tell us what happened from that time on until September 1992, approximately.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Practically, that was the beginning of occupation of Herzegovina and the beginning of preparations for the war and the attack on the village of Ravno, which is actually in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Today, it's the municipality of Ravno. And these were forces that later attacked the area of Dubrovnik in the Republic of Croatia. I stayed in the Police Administration as an adviser of Mr. Lucic, and at that time, since there were major forces of the JNA in that area, we were frequently in contact with them, and at the same time in late 1992, that area actually was significant to me because that was when I first began to have contacts with the European Union monitors and UN monitors who had arrived to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herzegovina to see what was going on with the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, in order to be very precise, can you tell us what your capacity was when you communicated with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: The initial contacts that I had with them, I was still the adviser of Mr. Lucic. This was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And he was what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of police of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, very well. Can you please tell us what happened then? We're now going up to September 1992. Did you transfer to a different agency after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: No, I stayed in the police because this attack on Ravno in September 1991 marked the beginning of the war, and practically the forming of the HV [as interpreted] in April 1992 actually took place in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I stayed in the police because the Internal Affairs Department of the Croatian Community of Herzegovina [as interpreted] was the first department that actually began to function and to be organised pursuant to the adopted regulations. So I remained in the police practically until the end of August or beginning of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In page 11, line 1, it is stated "HV," and the witness stated "HVO." Thanks, Madam Alaburic, for the assistance. Witness, you mentioned the HVO, not the Croatian Army, HV?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did you come to work for the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the beginning of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who invited you to come to work to the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic. I had known him. We had worked together at the MUP for a time while I was in Mostar, in the Mostar police, and Mr. Stojic at the time was assistant of the minister of the interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say that he invited you to come over to work, to use your expertise. When did you get your appointment and to which post in the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I started work without any appointment, formal establishment. I think that the formal appointment occurred on a session of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna sometime in mid-January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To which post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Assistant chief of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Deputy head.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did you leave that post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I was on that post as long as Mr. Stojic was the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before the appointment to the deputy head of Defence Department, had you been appointed to any other body of the HVO of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, practically, the first formal appointment was to -- as a member of the Commission for the Relationship with UNPROFOR of the HVO of HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I'm making this pause so that my questions and your answers can be reflected in the transcript. Let's go back to the Defence Department. What did you do after you arrived there? Sorry. What did you do there after Mr. Stojic left the department, so that we go through the whole of your career there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Stojic left, there were some proposals that I join the government in certain capacities. In cooperation with Mr. Prlic, I agreed to be appointed to the head of the Office for Cooperation with UNPROFOR, the European Community Monitoring Mission, and other international organisations; but I must highlight here that at the proposal of Mr. Perica Jukic or at his request, I performed some duties in the Personnel Administration, duties and tasks I had performed while I acted in my capacity as deputy chief of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So for a time, you performed both those duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was appointed head of the UNPROFOR, ECMM, other international organisations cooperation in December, and Mr. Jukic, who was newly appointed as the minister of defence for the Croatian Republic of HB, he asked me to remain there to help further development of the Personnel Administration and to continue performing all the tasks that I had performed while I was the deputy chief of the Defence of Department. In his words, "I have to find a new person to fill your shoes," and to which I answered, "Well, let me see with Mr. Prlic first." I did so, and Mr. Prlic told me that I'm duty-bound to perform the tasks of the new office and that I had my work cut out to develop that office, and if I could perform some other duties along the way, he would not object to that. But what he wanted was for that office to function properly, and this is why I considered to work in parallel on two positions, although I have to state that I was never appointed deputy or assistant minister of defence for personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, how long was Mr. Jukic minister of defence and who replaced him and when, and did you continue to cooperate with that other person in the same way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic stayed there briefly, a couple of months; I'm not sure whether three or three and a half months. I know it was a very short time. And Mr. Vladimir Soljic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Coric"] was appointed to replace him as minister of defence, a person I had long known. We came from the same hometown of Siroki Brijeg. I explained to him the arrangements with Mr. Jukic that I had made, in terms of my assistance to set up the personnel and care department or administration. He told me that I should be patient before an appropriate person is found to replace me, but unfortunately this took much longer than we had initially agreed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, until -- what was the period when you worked in the Office for Cooperation with the UNPROFOR, ECMM and International Organisation of HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Federal Government was set up pursuant to the Washington Agreement. There was the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe the Chamber knows how it functioned. The true setup of government started after the Dayton Accords, which means that my office worked approximately until March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say the following: That I do appreciate Ms. Nozica's efforts to slow down, but she also asked for the witness; but I would also like to ask Mr. Bozic to be kind enough to cooperate and to wait until Madam Nozica actually finishes her question, since we have, of course, in three languages interpretation, and then to answer only when the interpreters finish their job. So, therefore, I would like again to ask both of you to slow down a bit and to wait between the questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, let us correct the transcript. Page 13, line 20, what is stated is "Vladimir Coric." What should be stated there is "Vladimir Soljic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a mistake in my transcript. It is Valentin Coric [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This has been corrected, Mr. Bozic. Let's go back to March 1996. After that time, after the Dayton Accords, as you say, what was your next position?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the colleague. The witness said that it wasn't Valentin Coric, but on page 14, line 25, what is said in the transcript is "this is Valentin Coric." What I would like to ask the witness is to say what is the name of the person he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed, although I do not use the English language, to my detriment, that the transcript reflected "Valentin Coric," but what I said clearly and loudly was Vladimir Soljic, S-o-l-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, please, if you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it. After that while -- for a while I worked as an adviser or an external associate of Mr. Vladimir Soljic, who had been elected as president of the Federation, and with Mr. Ivo Andric Luzanski, who was also president of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If you do not mind, I can assist you during the first break, in terms of the names and surnames, because they -- the transcript is erroneous in this respect. So we do not correct it here during the session. Mr. Bozic, you told us where you work now. My question concerning this part of an introduction in your career, the last question in that part is whether you have ever been a member of the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I have never been a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I know, Mr. Bozic, that you had to hear many instructions. Do not ignore the instruction to wait for the question to enter into the transcript before answering, so that we do not overlap. Mr. Bozic, do you know when Mr. Soljic was appointed as head of the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I think it was in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know, and you said that you had known him from before, what were his positions before that appointment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know, because we used to bump into each other. He used to be assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell us his positions before that position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: If you mean the Ministry of the Interior, well, he worked there while I was in Mostar police, as assistant minister. I think that his post was labelled "supplies, financial and other affairs."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, until which date Mr. Stojic was head of Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a date that I remember. Until the 10th of November, 1993, when it was published on TV news what the composition of the new government will be, and I remember that event well. Mr. Stojic had this information on TV while he was watching a news bulletin together with his family, his parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, do you know when Mr. Stojic handed over his duty to the newly-appointed minister and whether, from the 10th of November onwards until the hand-over, did he come to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: He did not come to visit the Defence Department from the 10th of November onwards. I was shown a document co-signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Jukic on the hand-over, and this was dated 15th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, where was the Defence Department located? Where were its premises? Let me remind you that in mid-September, you came to the Defence Department. Can you tell us, from your arrival there until the 10th of November, 1993, where were the premises of the Defence Department located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: The first premises were in the building housing the Agronomy Institute or, better put, a major agro-business enterprise, Apro. We were housed there until after the conflict between Croats and Muslims in Mostar broke out. After that, we moved to several locations. One of those locations was a private house in Cim. Another location briefly was in a private home on the Mostar-Siroki Brijeg road. The third one was at Citluk, within a factory site. After that, we returned to Mostar. And when the Ministry was established and Mr. Lukic came, the then Ministry of Defence moved to Posusje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, could you tell us, when did you leave the first location and when did you return to it, roughly the time of the year, maybe month, as far as your recollection serves you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I believe that we left the initial premises in Mostar maybe mid-May, June, and we returned late summer, beginning of autumn, maybe September, maybe October. I can't be specific, but this is as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How many people worked in the office of the head of Department of Defence, just his office, at the time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: There was the secretary, then the driver and bodyguard in one. I was there, and an administrator later came to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you left the Defence Department, how many people had been employed in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: A handful of people, technical staff who worked there. I must tell you one thing. It wasn't easy to find the right people to work in the Defence Department because of the needs for people to be employed elsewhere because some people thought that the Defence Department could work with fewer personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, what was your job when you came to the Defence Department in early September 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I remember that my first jobs were, together with the colleagues who were already in the Personnel Administration before me, to draft a decision on the structuring of the Defence Department pursuant to the previous decision about the organisation of the Defence Ministry adopted by Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you had some colleagues there from the Personnel Department. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber when this Personnel Department was formed and who were these colleagues? How many of them were there who were helping you in these tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: The Personnel Department was formed before the forming of the Defence Department. I think this was sometime in May 1992, and there were three people working there. I know, for one, that he was a lawyer, one was a professor, and I'm not sure about the third person because I cannot remember what his profession was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you said that they were helping you at the beginning and that you were working on the decision on the establishment pursuant to a decision adopted by the president of the HZ-HB. Did you work on any other regulations at that time, let's say, in the course of October?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct the -- what you said. You said the decision, the basis for establishment, this was adopted by Mr. Boban, but I said that we adopted our decision on the establishment of the administration on the basis of the decision adopted by Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I understood what you said, and I just wanted to ask you what were perhaps any other documents that you worked on in October, if you did.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Since the Law on the Armed Forces was adopted before the Defence Department was established, in a certain amount of time there was a need for things to evolve and to expand; and I know that I worked on the drafting of a text on the amendments and additions to the Law on the Armed Forces, which if I can remember correctly was adopted at this meeting. It was the last meeting of the Presidency of the HZ-HB on the 18th of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bozic, what did you then do later? Were you charged specifically with some duties after this, and what were those duties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was formally still not deputy head of Defence Department, but I continued to work on my job pursuant to the decision on the establishment of the Defence Department and the defence section. And in view of the work that we were supposed to do and in view of the fact that the civilian sector actually was under the jurisdiction of the Personnel Administration, the bulk of my work was actually to coordinate of the work -- to coordinate the work of the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, were you the only lawyer in the Defence Department? And I'm not including here other organisational units, only the office of Mr. Stojic. Were you the only lawyer in that office which we described earlier? I'm not talking about the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the only lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, after you were appointed deputy head of the Defence Department, did you work on documents that were drafted or adopted by the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And did you work by yourself or were you assisted by these persons from the Personnel Department and from other lawyers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had help from my colleagues who worked in the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move to a new subject. I'm going to ask you, Mr. Bozic, if you took part in the arming or providing weapons to the Croatian and Bosniak people in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a few questions of a pure logistical nature to put to you on paper, pens and erasers, in order to better understand a few issues that the Judges of this Trial Chamber will have to think about. You will understand my questions, of course, because from your experience, I observed that you were a judge, a prosecutor. You were also a chief of police in Mostar. You had very high positions. Therefore, I'm sure you will be able to answer my questions. When you were appointed within the Defence Department, if I understood correctly, you were appointed because you knew Mr. Stojic. Did he recruit yourself -- did he recruit you, himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Stojic told me that he was forming that department, and knowing what I did before in the police and knowing my experience as a lawyer, he said that it would be good to have such a person there. I don't want to seem immodest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guess you had an office. Was your office far away from his?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Our two offices were actually separated by the office where the secretary was sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Between your office and his, there was the secretary, so you weren't far away from Mr. Stojic. We know that one of your duties was personnel issues. Could you please tell me how many people belonged to that department; 50 people, 100? Could you give me a ballpark figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I'm in a position to respond to your question at all, I first have to say one thing. It's a fact from that time, the Personnel Administration was formed in 1992, regardless of -- in May, regardless of the department, and that personnel section was working, as you can see, on the basis of reports that were drafted for the second half of 1992, on registering those who were killed, wounded, missing combatants, and also on securing assistance to the families of the killed, missing and wounded fighters; and practically the Personnel Administration, when I began to work with them, together with my colleagues, actually had not yet began to deal with these matters that you are speaking about. As time went by, perhaps starting from March 1993, when the number of employees grew in the administration, the Personnel Administration still did its work regarding welfare, also moved on to assignments that originally were supposed to be in its jurisdiction, but it did continue to record the employees within the Defence Department, also registered members of the units, and later began to issue IDs to members of the HVO. So this was a process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you, Witness. One moment, please, because your answer took three minutes, and then it will be said that Judges' questions are too long, whilst my question only took a few seconds, whilst your answer was very long. I did not want to ask you about what you were doing. It was a very specific question. How many staff in the Defence Department? I said 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, a thousand. Give me an approximate figure. That's all I need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I have to just say that it is very important to know which period we are referring to. Which period are you asking about regarding the number of employees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... said that there was an increase, that you started with 5, we ended with 50 employees. That's all I want to know. I just want a figure. How many to start with, and how many on the 10th of November, 1993, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Taking into account that the Defence Administration had its sectors, then I would need to come out with the numbers in these sectors. I'm afraid that I really could not be accurate, and I don't want to guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just approximately. Fifty? I'm not asking for a precise figure. Just approximately. Well, just say you don't know and I can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, so you're not going to answer. As to the people working in that Defence Department, did you have together with you military personnel, people in uniform, with weapons? Did you have military people with you or were there only civilians working in the department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking if I had a uniform, at that time we were all wearing uniforms, both civilians and military personnel. It was the times. Within the Defence Department, I think that we didn't actually have any military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's the main question. You have just said that in the Defence Department, there were no military, so even if you wore uniforms, I wanted to know whether around Mr. Stojic there were officers, captains, majors, colonels, generals who had their offices just next to his.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about the sectors, I was talking about sectors within the Defence Administration -- Department. There was also the Main Staff, so everything that I am telling you about the military personnel, I am talking about the sectors that were within the Defence Administration; but I'm not taking into account the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are asking you to be closer to your microphones. You have two in front of you. Yes, yes, pull them towards you. Thank you. If I understood properly, in the Defence Department, later to become the Defence Ministry, there were no military personnel, there were no officers who would have had military positions. Is that how things should be understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now my last question. In those various premises that you mentioned, was there one room with military maps in it where the various units or HVO brigades were positioned? Was there somebody who, on a minute-by-minute basis or an hourly basis, would position the units on the map so that Mr. Stojic knew, in realtime, what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that there was any kind of General Staff of the sort that you are talking about in the area that we are talking about, but I did say that within the department, there was a Main Staff; but not as a General Staff in the sense that I understand you to mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, in relation to Judge Antonetti's question about the number of employees in the Defence Department, I asked you a specific question about how many employees there were in the office, the inner circle around Mr. Stojic, and you said that there were five to seven people, at the most. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question like that, and this is what I answered. As for Judge Antonetti's question, I said that that would need to be also the total number of all employees in the other sectors as well, so I didn't wish to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I understood your question, but I just wanted to say that when we come to the internal structure and organisation, we will cover that in more detail and try to provide an answer, if you can remember it. There was a question also, Mr. Bozic, about your eventual participation or securing of weapons to the Croatian and Bosniak people in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I did take part, together with colleagues from the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo and colleagues from the Mostar police, and I must say here, without going into names - I don't want to omit anyone - that the key job in that work was Mr. Delimustafic and his assistant, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, we're talking about 1991. Why was it necessary to arm the Croat and Bosniak people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Their Honours know that in the area of the former Yugoslavia, at that time the Yugoslav People's Army had confiscated the weapons from the Territorial Defence, and in a symbolic sense confiscated weapons from the people themselves. And in view of the circumstances in the Republic of Croatia, there was a sense that hard times were ahead and that it was important to try, as far as this was possible, to arm the Croatian and the Muslim people, and one of the legal ways, conditionally speaking, was to do that was the Ministry of the Interior, which had its own reserve force that was fortunately not disarmed by the Yugoslav People's Army. And so using this reserve police force, there was a legal option, through the Bosnia-Herzegovina Defence Ministry, to arm the Muslim and the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And can you tell us of any other ways, that you are aware of, of obtaining weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that here, and I believe that Your Honours know that, that the Croats and the Muslims were aware of the times and they provided -- they obtained weapons for themselves, costing thousands of German marks. People were finding ways of getting weapons, themselves. In view of everything that was going on in the Republic of Croatia, the transfer of large forces of the JNA from Slovenia and from Croatia, there was a sense of impending war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, would you like to explain to the Trial Chamber what was your specific role in the arming? I'm reminding you of the Pasaga [as interpreted] statement which implicated highly-positioned officials of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was your role in all that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Reserve forces' weapons were, for a time, warehoused at regional police and local police stations. That regional was the Mostar regional police headquarters, and the central warehouse stocked a large quantity of weapons in the central warehouse of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Mr. Delimustafic and Mr. Stojic allowed for those weapons to be distributed, among others, to the police in Mostar. Everything was regular, in terms of paperwork and regulations. And after the weapons were received at Mostar, those weapons were distributed to both the Muslims and Croats in the area of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say, in your last sentence, that it was distributed to Croats and Muslims. It was not distributed to the Serbs. How do you see your actions of the day, and what was your motive to take part in that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Trial Chamber and any other observer may form an opinion that such actions may lack professionality, and that they may seem immoral to work in a state organ representing all of the citizens of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina republic, and practically to commit actions that the same body of government should sanction. In other words, to distribute arms and weapons and commit offences which that body of government is working to eradicate. But for myself, in my opinion and opinion of all the colleagues that I worked on that with, was that this was the only possible, reasonable, and justifiable reaction to what had happened before. As far as I personally am concerned, on top of what was happening in the Republic of Croatia, that I described, my first decision was, when all the mask [Realtime transcript read in error, "mosques"] fell, that events which really bared the situation for me was when tanks -- JNA tanks came to Siroki Brijeg and when the police that I headed detected arms which the JNA had distributed in Eastern Herzegovina in the municipality of Bileca, of course distributing those weapons to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what do you mean by the event with the tanks in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: It was an event which had, and I believe, it will have an historical significance. My take on that event was particular to me. I was then still chief of police in Mostar. When I was phoned by the mayor of Siroki Brijeg, my hometown, Mr. Andjelko Mikulic, his voice was a tremble, he said: "What are they doing to us? I'm telling you, they will not pass this point. They're not going to Croatia, and they're not going to occupy us here."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, could you specify the date of that event, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Of course I can. From the 7th to the -- 5th to the 7th May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention. In the transcript, page 28, line 5, you said "the mosques fell."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What is in the transcript is something completely different. If need be, you may later on explain what you meant by those words. You can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. On that very point, I would object and ask for clarification. What the transcript, at least in English says, it says exactly that, and I don't know what the discrepancy seen by counsel is. It says "all the mosques fell," and there's no indication of what Mr. Bozic means, or the time, or the location. And I think that we should not go forward without some explanation for that statement, and putting time and place on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. While in the French, it was not "mosques," but "masks." So there must be a problem somewhere, a hitch somewhere. I've already pointed it out. People working from B/C/S into English have got to be very careful to what people say in B/C/S, because mosques and masks, that's not the same thing. Can you please confirm what you said, Witness? Witness, what did you say, exactly? Did you mention mosques or masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't speak English. I can't understand, but I'm very fluent in Croatian, and the words "maska," "mask" and "dzamija," "mosque," are not even closely resembling one another, so I'm really at a loss how this may have happened in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you say, did you say "masks" or "mosques."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "masks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you satisfied, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I hope the Chamber and everyone agrees it was worthwhile to get that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Go ahead. Witness, we were then on the 7th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7th of May. Very well. 7th of May, 1991. On that day, did Yugoslavia still exist as a state? On the 7th of May, 1991, was Croatia independent, was Bosnia and Herzegovina independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Yugoslavia still existed. Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were recognised in 1992, recognised by the International Community, and entered the UN. At that time, Yugoslavia still existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you said that the masks fell or were about to fall, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I illustrated, by those two events, when I said the masks had fallen, it was believed that Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to be Yugoslav and people's. It was supposed to work for Yugoslavia and work for the benefit of all the peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, you started explaining how the mayor of Siroki Brijeg phoned you. You said that it took place on the 7th of May, 1991. Please continue with your account of what happened afterwards. We are proceeding very slowly, so please be as concise as possible, describing your first event with the tanks.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: After that, I asked an associate to check what was going on: After that, I asked a colleague of mine to look into that situation, what was going on in the city, and briefly afterwards, I received information that a large column of tanks and trucks had passed through the town, in the direction of Siroki Brijeg; that they destroyed curb-stones and tree-lines in the city of Mostar on their way, en route. And after a while, we received further information that the people in the location of Polog stopped that tank column. Police started performing their duties in terms of providing security and finding alternative routes for the traffic to continue. They started securing that site so as to prevent any incidents from occurring. And in the afternoon hours, Mr. Stjepan Kljujic, member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency, arrived there, in the company of Mr. Jerko Doko, minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and briefly afterwards gentlemen Mate Boban and a group of members of Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived shortly afterwards, because BiH Parliament was in session on that day. I arrived there for the first time with Mr. Kljujic, Mr. Doko, Mr. Boban, and the MPs, so a large group of people who did not allow Mr. Kljujic to address them because he asked them to let the tanks through. After that, I returned to my office in Mostar. Late in the evening, while Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Doko and their associates were at my office, I received word from the reception that a JNA general wanted to talk to me. His name was Zorc.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I apologise -- I apologise for interrupting you. You are explaining this in a very concise manner, but you are speaking very slow. You may speed up. This is too slow. The interpreters and transcript will catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zorc, which is not a characteristic of a general, in my opinion, was looking very apprehensive when he came to the office. He said that he did not know what was going on, why this column of tanks moved in the first place. He said that he was in Slovenia for the weekend when it happened, and since tensions were high, everything had to be done to prevent even the smallest incidents from sparking up because it may have catastrophic consequences. So patrols were organised of policemen and civilians who were working on preventing such incidents from happening on that night and throughout the night. Mr. Kljujic, the following day, managed to establish contact with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and he requested that he come to Mostar to convene a session of the Committee for General People's Defence and Social Self-Defence. It was the highest body at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dealing with defence and civil protection. There were several conversations between them. One particularly stuck in my memory, when Mr. Kljujic told Mr. Izetbegovic: "If you do not come to Mostar, from tomorrow on Croatian members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and members of Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina will become opposition, will cross the floor." Another interesting situation occurred on that same day which showed the conduct of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. Mr. Kljujic, Mr. Doko and their colleagues were invited to a meeting to the JNA barracks in Mostar, and they went there. After a while, my secretary told me that there was a call from President Tudjman's Cabinet, who wanted to establish urgent contact with Mr. Kljujic. I relayed to our services the need to contact our officers escorting Mr. Kljujic, Mr. Doko, and their colleagues; but soon afterwards I received feedback that no contact could be made, that our means of communications were jammed. It was perfectly clear to me, what was going on. I asked a colleague of mine to go to the barracks in plain clothes and to tell Mr. Kljujic that he was supposed to come to my office urgently, which Mr. Kljujic did subsequently, and I told him, Mr. Kljujic, when he returned: "You, as a member of the Presidency, which is part of a collective commander having jurisdiction over the defence of this country, were held captive by the JNA, obviously with the intent for you to be isolated and be blocked in your efforts to try to find a solution to this problem."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Ms. Nozica, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, we stopped at the time when Mr. Kljujic went to the JNA barracks, and I would like you to continue, but at the same time I would like to ask you to speak a little bit faster and to be as concise as possible and complete this topic, because time is flying by, and I'm afraid that we won't have enough time to cover other topics. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, you will start -- can you please start again, because your microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: It was the second day, when the tanks were stopped, the situation in the area was very tense, and that whole day JNA helicopters and planes were over-flying or flying low over the area of Herceg-Bosna, parachutes were dropping in that region; and it could have been quite a serious situation. Mr. Kljujic insisted that Mr. Izetbegovic comes, and then he came on the third day, and then he came to Mostar. He came to my office. Now I'm going to say something publicly that I have never said openly so far. Mr. Izetbegovic, who at that time was with Minister Delimustafic and, I think, with Mr. Stojic, Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, too, who's the president of the Herzegovina SDA, said, and I will try to paraphrase him, in his well-known style, speaking quietly, You know, this is my greatest personal and political risk, greater than the one I had and experienced in prisons during Communism. And then he said that the day before, he had gone to a joint Presidency meeting in Belgrade, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, when the then minister of defence of Yugoslavia, General Kadijevic, told him that he should not get involved in any of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting the witness, but given the discussions that we've had in recent days, I must point out to the Chamber none of this is covered in the 65 ter summary for this witness. There's nothing about going into these sorts of matters, this history. This is a complete surprise to the Prosecution. Exactly given the reasons and the points the Chamber has noted in the past days about the necessity of fully adequate summaries that comply with the law, this is a complete surprise and is not covered anywhere in the four summaries that have been provided by the Stojic Defence. We object to this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, it seems that you are addressing the issue of the intervention of the JNA in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it seems that in the summary, this issue has not been explicitly referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to stress that these events, and specifically this event, the participation of Mr. Bozic, were covered by Mr. Kljujic here on the 9th of October, 2006, and Mr. Bozic's name is mentioned on page 8015, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Nozica. This was not the question. The question was: Where, in your 65 ter information, do you refer to this subject and announce that the witness will talk about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I stated in the summary that the witness is going to discuss his role in the arming of the Croatian and the Muslim people. The witness, as part of this topic, replies that it is his motive to participate in that was actually this event and another event. So this refers to the 65 ter summary note on the topic of arming of the Croat and Muslim people. The witness himself said that he was motivated by these two events to participate in the arming, and I wanted to say that this first event cannot be a surprise for the Prosecution because Mr. Kljujic spoke about that in the courtroom here and mentioned Mr. Bozic when he was discussing it. For that reason, I believe that, first of all, it's a topic that was announced, and, secondly, it's an event that is familiar to everyone in the courtroom because it was discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you're complaining because you don't have enough time. You've warned the witness because he had to be more specific in his answers. You're talking about something that everybody here has already discussed. I don't think it is necessary for the witness to expand on the fact that the JNA intervene and that it led to different positions at the individual level. I think you'd better ask him, What do you know about the JNA; and then he would have said, well, The JNA intervened. And then you could have asked, Did it have any repercussion on your own participation? And then he would have given you a specific answer. And then you could have moved on to another topic. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to put a line under what Judge Trechsel said. The fact of what another witness may have talked about previously, including Mr. Kljujic, is no justification whatsoever for not putting it in the 65 ter summary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. To follow up on what Mr. Scott has just said, in the 65 ter summary you should have said that Mr. Kljujic -- because Mr. Kljujic had mentioned this, the witness would come and add to what had just been said by Mr. Stojic. You haven't done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I accept your suggestion. It's true that we didn't do that. But as far as I understood things, I asked the witness what motivated him to take part in the arming of the Croatian and the Muslim people, and so this motive was part of that whole topic. I am going to ask for your indulgence and ask the witness to finish off this first topic, if you permit. He did say that there were two events. The first is the situation in Prolom, and the second one was when the JNA was arming the Serbian people. So I'm going to ask him to very briefly complete this topic and explain the second one, and that is as part of his motivation to act in the way that he explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, you heard I have just -- that is why I was actually trying to speed you up a bit because I understand that your answers on the first topic took up a lot of time; so I would like you to finish very briefly, whether Mr. Izetbegovic addressed the people and what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but I consider it important to say what Mr. Izetbegovic said in my office then, and that was that General Kadijevic told him that he had nothing to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I object. I object to -- my same objection stands. The Chamber's not ruled to the contrary. This has nothing to do with the efforts of the JNA to take away arms or -- we'll agree to that, no dispute in the courtroom whatsoever. There's no disagreement in the courtroom whatsoever; the JNA, in 1991, made efforts to disarm both the Croat and the Muslim side. No dispute about that. Can we move on, and not go on to a topic on which there is complete surprise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there's no disagreement. Everybody agrees the JNA intervened. Now, for Mr. Stojic's Defence, what is important?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is exceptionally important for Mr. Stojic's Defence, now that you're asking, since the indictment does talk about joint criminal enterprise from 1991, that Mr. Stojic, together with this gentleman, took part in the arming of Croat and Muslim people in order to stand up to the JNA and then later to the aggression of the Bosnian Serbs. I believe this to be an extremely important detail that this witness is talking about and which we discussed or mentioned in our summary on the 65 ter list. I do take into account everything that has been said in the courtroom, but I would like to ask the witness to tell us very briefly how all this ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Izetbegovic address the people? And then we will move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Izetbegovic did address --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before the -- I apologise for interrupting interpretation, Your Honour; but I'm going to stand on this point, given the very points that have been raised recently about this, and that is the importance of this matter and getting fully adequate summaries. So I apologise if I'm trying the Chamber's patience. I do stand on this point. That is the point we've made repeatedly. If -- and I'll add this: If it is, as counsel says, exceptionally important, then presumably it was exceptionally important enough to be included in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will confer with my colleagues to see whether counsel can go on with her question about what Mr. Izetbegovic said to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will ask Ms. Nozica to move on to another issue and to address an issue that has been explicitly referred to in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the topic of arming that you undertook together - we're talking about the arming of the Croatian and the Muslim people - very briefly just follow my question. In the events that happened after that, did anything else happen that motivated you? But just please tell us in one sentence. You already did mention that, and the Prosecutor didn't object to that. You said, I will remind you, that the police discovered that the JNA was arming the Serbs in Stolac. Can you please answer if at that time you had contacts with any person, directly or indirectly, who worked on the arming of the Serbian people with weapons from the JNA? Did you have any contacts or did anyone ask you for contacts from the JNA to enable this arming to proceed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't in Stolac, actually. It was in Bileca where the police discovered that the JNA was arming the Serbs in Eastern Herzegovina. And then after this was discovered by the police, the Yugoslav People's Army or, better said, the officers who were in the JNA at the time prevented the police from doing their job, and they never allowed us to complete our police work. These were civilians, it was a civilian vehicle, and the policemen who discovered that recorded that in the truck there were crates with weapons from specific military posts of the Yugoslav People's Army to which this weaponry belonged.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, these two events which you described, were they directly connected to your decision to proceed with other members of the MUP and the Mostar police with the arming, as you said, of the Muslim and Croat people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't answer to the previous part of your question about whether there was anyone who prevented that. Yes, there was a person who did prevent that -- wanted to prevent that, and after that, that person got in touch with me. And then at some point in 1992, I found out that that person was prevented from an inquiry into this whole matter. This was done by somebody who was in the JNA, and his name was Fikret Muslimovic, and he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether these things affected your decision to assist in the arming of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In relation to this topic that we discussed relating to events or documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm sorry for interrupting, but you've just confirmed that it was decided to arm the Muslim population and the Croat population because the JNA had armed the Serbs. Who took the decision? Was it you? Who decided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question. Who do you mean, when you say, "Who decided?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the transcript, I read that "it was decided to arm the Muslims and the Croats." One may assume that you were the one who made the decision, you yourself, Mr. Bozic, or maybe other people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I said -- evidently there's a mistake in the transcript. I said the first time at the beginning and later, and now I'm saying that these two events were something that made me finally decide, and not only me but my other colleagues too, that something needed to be done to arm Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, Herzegovina, in view of everything that we knew about the conduct of the then Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, you -- you, who given those two events, decided to arm the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that that was my personal decision, and the main persons were -- I mean, who made it possible for the Serbs to get weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it was your decision. Nobody else decided for you that you were going to arm the Croats and the Muslims against those who were arming the Serbs. So you alone decided, of your own free will, that you were going to do so; there was no committee, there was no chief or head of anything, you were the one who decided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We misunderstood each other. At the beginning of my testimony, I said that looking from the outside perhaps it was unprofessional and immoral for someone working in the police, and we all did work in the police, to do something like that and to arm Muslims and Croats; but in view of these two events, I said - and it was a mistake in the transcript earlier - that masks fell, and I said that also before, that the key persons were Mr. Delimustafic, who was the defence minister -- Delimustafic, he was the MUP minister, and also Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, because there's a lot at stake here, if I understand properly, you, being in charge of the police, had a perception of the situation at the time, and you made the decision to arm your fellow Muslims and Croats because you had information according to which the JNA was arming the Serbs. And when you made that decision, it wasn't Mr. Boban asking you to make such decision, nor Mr. Stojic, nor Mr. Praljac [as interpreted], nor Mr. Tudjman, nor Mr. Bobekto, nor Mr. Susak, it was you alone who decided to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that I, myself, made the decision. I accepted to do a part of the work with my colleagues. The decision to provide or secure weapons was Mr. Stojic, who was the deputy -- assistant minister and Mr. Delimustafic, who was the minister. They made the decision, and we agreed to implement that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, all right. This is clearer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the documents as listed in binder 2D 00288. That's supposed to be the document at the top of the binder, please. Let me know when you find it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you recognise the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: This is the gentleman that I made reference to, when I said that I found out from a document dated 1992, that he was the person who prevented the police inquiries as to the illegal arming in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What is the date of this document, and do you know how Mr. Fikret Muslimovic, in his capacity as a highly-ranking JNA officer, was put into such a position, and do you have any information about his career, his path?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: It is known to me that in Muslim circles, there were frequent discussions about his arrival and about his position. I read several books about that, and I recall that from the book, the war diary of the deputy of staff commander of the Army of BiH, General Stjepan Siber, his memoirs entitled "Lies and Truths," it was stated in that book that Mr. Muslimovic climbed to a very high position in the Muslim forces and ended up in the cabinet of Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you take a look at the bottom part of this page and read out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it out, but I would like to make reference to this first part, making reference to Bileca and the crimes committed by the aggressors there, and the location where the weapons provided to the Serbs by the JNA were disclosed and prevented police forces to undertake inquiries, that all this was done by Mr. Fikret Muslimovic. The latter part of the page that you refer to makes mention -- makes mention of something that I saw for the first time in preparation for this testimony, when it speaks about assessment that further increase of tensions may be expected, including possible confrontation between the -- between ARBiH and HVO, it is very important to make the situation between Muslims and the HVO as passive as possible and to influence their transfer from the HVO to the Army of BiH, which brings me back to the events of the 30th of June, 1993. What I personally noticed, when I took a look at this document, was the date, the 16th of April, 1993, which is after the Vance-Owen Plan had been co-signed by Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic, after an agreement reached at New York on the establishment of a joint body by Mr. Ganic, Akmadzic, Boban, and some others. What struck me as significant concerning this document is on the 19th of April, 1993, at Medjugorje, there was a meeting convened between Generals Petkovic and General Halilovic, with the presence of General Morillon, on commencing the preparatory work for the establishment of joint command of HVO and Army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at another document, 2D 00033. It is the next document in your binder. Could you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. This explains how weapons were forwarded from the central warehouse of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Mostar, and I can see the very well-known-to-me signature of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is this a document which corroborates part of your testimony explaining how these weapons ended up where they ended up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: Exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then let's take a look at 2D 00976.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very briefly, we'll explain what this is. This is an excerpt from a book authored by Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic. Was this gentleman included in that activity, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for going back to the former document. This is a very complex issue, and we might get lost very easily. There is a document which seems to address the issue of weapons. This document comes from Sarajevo, it originates from Sarajevo, and it goes to Mostar. "CSB Mostar," that's what's written on the document. Now, I'm trying to understand what this document means. You seem to know what it means, so I'd like you to confirm my conclusions about this document. This document bears the date of the 20th of August, 1991. At that time, were instructions sent from Sarajevo so that weapons be given to the population? What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document shows that weapons left the central warehouse of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, specifies the type of weapons, the quantities of weapons, and states that the Centre for Security in Mostar, or the police in Mostar, is the recipient of the shipment. As I stated at the beginning of my testimony, this was the only so-called legal or legitimate way for the weapons to come from Sarajevo warehouse to Mostar and then to be distributed to the Muslims and the Croats from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, if I understand properly, in 1991 in Sarajevo, who was making the decision? Was it the president of the Presidency, was it the Presidency itself? Who decided, in Sarajevo, to send weapons to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, a key role was played by Minister Delimustafic and his assistant, Stojic, and I believe that everything was done with the cognisance of the Muslim and Croatian members of the Sarajevo government, the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Minister Delimustafic, was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And so these weapons were distributed to Muslims and Croats? Very well, thank you. I'm starting to understand better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the following document corroborates that. I wanted to work through those documents together with the witness to make it perfectly clear - we have an expert - excerpt from a book 2D 00976. This is a book authored by Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic entitled "Bosnian Muslim Political Show-down."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
